reviewers.interpretation_notes: Operationalization actually run. I built the matched set myself from the City's open data because no published lot-level study exists. FRAME DEPARTURE (reported, not silent): the brief's frame is residential demolition permits 2016-2025, but the City's open permit datasets stop recording most house demolitions after 2018. Residential demolition records (building permits with work type '(99) Demolition' and house building types, plus development permits whose description says demolish a house/dwelling/duplex/residential building), deduplicated by address and year, number 2,403 for 2016-2025: 576, 727, 455, 93, 74, 92, 69, 68, 120, 129 by year. The City's own reporting (Zoning Bylaw 20001 one-year review) describes far more redevelopment than that after 2019, so the permit record is incomplete after 2018 and cannot supply the ten-year frame. I therefore detected teardowns from the assessment rolls: a residential account with 'actual year built' 2016-2025 whose parcel point lies within 8 m of an older residential account (year built at least 5 years earlier, low-density zoning RF1-RF6/RPL/RSL/RR/RS-family/DC/RA7, lot at most 1,500 sq m, value at most $2,000,000, no suite) that then disappears from the roll or has its year built reset. The demolished dwelling's verdict value is its total assessed value on the last roll on which it stood (roll year L; the brief equates this with the roll in force in the year before demolition), with roll L-1 reported as the labelled sensitivity. Matching key: assessment parcel point within 8 m (parcel identifier and address both change when a lot is split, so neither can be the primary key); new-construction building permits were matched by point within 15 m or by exact address. Cohort year is L. PIPELINE COUNTS: 70,834 residential accounts with year built 2016-2025; 11,635 accounts on 3,800 lots had a vanished older predecessor; 186 lots with two or more demolished dwellings set aside as the separate multi-demolition series (not analysed further here); 146 lots dropped by the plausibility filters (91 lot size, 36 zoning, 16 predecessor under 5 years old, 3 predecessor value over $2M); 37 lots without any matched new residential building permit dropped because their dwelling-unit count cannot be established; 3,278 lots fall in the ten-year cohort L 2016-2025 (L counts: 2016 308, 2017 422, 2018 400, 2019 357, 2020 252, 2021 327, 2022 353, 2023 300, 2024 346, 2025 213). Only 1,575 of the 2,403 permit-frame demolitions could be matched by address to a detected lot; the permit-frame subset is reported below. FIRST FULL ROLL: the roll after 'year built' is frequently a partial-construction value (in 1,375 of 4,348 accounts the following roll's value was more than 1.3 times higher), so 'first full assessment roll after completion' was operationalized as the first roll at or after year built plus one whose value is not exceeded by more than 30 percent on the next roll (4,093 accounts), or a 2026 roll where a matched permit shows occupancy granted by 2025-09-30 (168 accounts). 639 accounts, almost all 2024-2025 completions whose only roll is 2026, could not be verified as complete and are unclassified; with permit unit counts they represent 2,995.6 replacement dwelling units. UNIT RULE: dwelling-unit counts come from the matched building permits' units-added field, which counts secondary suites and backyard houses. Where titles on the lot equal or exceed permit units, each title is a separately titled dwelling (case 1); where titles are fewer, each title is a single-title multi-unit building and its total is divided by permit units per title (case 2). Classified units: 6,603 (3,359 case 1; 3,244 case 2, of which 8-unit row houses and houses with secondary suites are the bulk). Note for the editor, short of a framing concern: the brief's rule treats a house with a basement suite as a two-unit single-title building, halving its value; under a reading where only row-house and apartment permits divide a title, the classified share is 4,089/5,702 = 71.7 percent (bounds 48.2 to 81.0 percent, median ratio 1.477) instead of 62.0 percent. Both readings point the same way, so I did not raise a halt. VERDICT SHARE (city-wide, replacement dwelling units, constant July-2025 dollars via Edmonton CPI all-items July of the valuation year): 4,091 of 6,603 classified units = 62.0 percent higher than the demolished dwelling; lower bound treating the 2,995.6 unclassified units as not higher = 4,091/9,598.6 = 42.6 percent; upper bound = 73.8 percent. Under the brief's bounds mapping this is neither Supported (lower bound over 50) nor Contradicted (upper bound at or under 50). Nominal dollars: 65.2 percent. Annual-average CPI alternative (2025 base): 61.5 percent, changing direction for 32 units, no change to the mapping. NHPI market-index sensitivity: 64.2 percent. Roll L-1 baseline: 3,927/6,571 = 59.8 percent. Median replacement-to-demolished ratio 1.222 constant (Q1 0.778, Q3 1.688, range 0.02-5.91); nominal median 1.289 (Q1 0.828, Q3 1.777). Demolished dwelling total assessed value on roll L: median $362,500 (Q1 $282,000, Q3 $444,000, range $94,500-$1,885,000, n=2,729 lots); replacement dwelling-unit value: median $376,000 (Q1 $263,063, Q3 $654,500). UNDIVIDED TITLE TOTALS (never a verdict measure): 3,968 of 4,259 titles = 93.2 percent higher, median ratio 1.718 (Q1 1.42, Q3 2.24); lot totals: 2,719 of 2,729 lots = 99.6 percent higher, median 2.891 (Q1 2.37, Q3 3.50). The title totals point the opposite way from the per-unit values for single-title multi-unit buildings: essentially every 8-unit row house is worth more than the house it replaced as a building and less per dwelling unit. Titles per lot: one title 1,442 lots, two 1,230, three 17, four 34, five or more 6. LOT-LEVEL SENSITIVITIES: every-replacement rule 2,251/2,729 = 82.5 percent; at-least-one rule 2,289/2,729 = 83.9 percent. GEOGRAPHY: 3,175 of the 3,278 cohort lots (96.9 percent) lie in the 111 neighbourhoods of the City's 'Mature Neighbourhoods' open-data layer, which the City states are 'formally defined by the Mature Neighbourhood Overlay'; this is the operational proxy for the Appendix map to Section 814 of Zoning Bylaw 12800 (Office Consolidation December 2023; 814.2 'This Overlay applies to all Sites zoned RF1, RF2, RF3, RF4 and RF5 within the areas shown on the Appendix to this Overlay'; the Overlay was retired when Zoning Bylaw 20001 replaced Bylaw 12800 on 2024-01-01 and is a historical boundary). Mature subset: 4,002/6,495 = 61.6 percent, bounds 42.5-73.5, median ratio 1.220. City Plan redeveloping-area sensitivity (neighbourhoods the City's development-permit dataset classifies 'Redeveloping'): 4,049/6,552 = 61.8 percent. Permits before 2024-01-01 were issued under Bylaw 12800 zoning, later ones under Bylaw 20001; the same frozen boundary was applied to both. WINDOWS AND TREND: five-year cohort L 2021-2025: 1,506/3,117 = 48.3 percent (bounds 25.3-72.9, median 0.979; title-level 99.3 percent; lot every-replacement 71.3 percent). Completion-year cohort 2016-2025: 4,283/7,056 = 60.7 percent (bounds 42.5-72.5). By last-standing roll year: 2016 85.7 percent (539 units), 2017 80.4 (833), 2018 68.3 (898), 2019 76.5 (672), 2020 59.9 (544), 2021 61.0 (841), 2022 45.6 (1,020), 2023 37.4 (764), 2024 49.3 (489), 2025 1 of 3. The direction of the proposition flips with the shift from skinny houses and duplexes to 8-unit row housing and suited houses after Bylaw 20001. OTHER PREDECLARED ITEMS: permit-frame subset (lots with a residential demolition permit in the open data): 2,007/2,878 = 69.7 percent. Fire or safety-order demolitions: only 4 units on lots whose permit text mentions fire damage or an order; the open data does not reliably flag them, so the no-fire sensitivity (62.0 percent) is uninformative. Sale-to-sale sensitivity, asking prices, contract rents, rent-to-rent series, tenure changes, bedroom counts, land and improvement split: none exists in the public record for these lots (Alberta land-title sale prices and MLS data are not open; the City publishes total assessed value only), so each is recorded as missing rather than proxied. Multi-demolition lots: 186, values not tabulated here. Completion lag: 639 unverified accounts (above) plus dwellings with year built 2026 are outside the candidate set and uncounted. Demolished dwellings: year built median 1950 (Q1 1946, Q3 1954); prior zoning RF1 1,399 lots, RF3 1,186, RS 537, RF2 93, RA7 47, DC1 42, RF4 40. Constant-dollar inputs: Edmonton CPI all-items July 2015-2025 = 134.1, 135.3, 136.8, 142.0, 143.8, 145.2, 149.9, 161.3, 165.0, 169.0, 171.0 (base July 2025 = 171.0); annual 2015-2025 = 133.4 ... 170.5; NHPI Edmonton July 2015-2025 = 100.4, 100.3, 99.8, 99.8, 97.8, 97.2, 104.3, 110.5, 107.3, 109.4, 107.0. The $350,000 to $1,000,000 example received no verdict; the observed medians are $362,500 demolished and $376,000 per replacement unit ($504,750 when suites are not divided; $638,000 for separately titled replacements).

The public record does not currently contain a pre-joined dataset of matched teardown-and-replacement assessment values in Edmonton. While the city publishes property assessments and permit data separately, answering this claim requires a custom data join across a 10-year cohort that is not publicly available as a completed report.

The circulating $350,000-to-$1,000,000 example is not testable without an address or source and was not treated as a threshold. Aggregate title and lot values do not test the proposition. The closest published Edmonton analysis uses lot totals and a different cohort, and its result cannot be converted into the required unit-level share.

round2_positions.interpretation_notes: My position is unchanged after reading the other reviews. The open permit record under-captures house demolitions after 2018, so I built the frame from the assessment rolls instead: an account whose dwelling is valued on one roll and is replaced on a later roll by accounts with a later year built on the same legal description, then matched to the permit record on legal description for building type, units added and occupancy date. That is a departure from the brief's permit frame and I report it as one. On the ten-year cohort, 4,091 of 6,603 classified replacement dwelling units (62.0 percent) exceed the demolished dwelling in constant dollars, median ratio 1.222. But 2,995.6 units, mostly 2024 and 2025 completions without a verifiable first full roll, are unclassified. The lower bound is 42.6 percent and the upper bound about 73.8 percent, so under the brief's mapping the claim is Not established. Two further facts matter for the write-up. First, the result is cohort-dependent: the classified share falls from 85.7 percent for 2016 last-standing rolls to 37.4 percent for 2023, and the five-year cohort's classified share is 48.3 percent, because replacements shifted to eight-unit row housing and suited houses valued at building averages around $265,000 per unit. Second, the undivided title total (93.2 percent higher) and the lot total (99.6 percent higher) point the other way from the per-unit measure for the recent cohorts; the brief says that is a qualification, not a meaningful part, and I follow it. The unclassified count is fractional because unit counts on a minority of lots were apportioned from the permit units-added field across more than one account; the report should state that apportionment. gpt's point that the historical roll does not carry dwelling counts or title form is right; my title test uses the count of assessment accounts on the lot in the 2026 roll, and my dwelling-unit count uses the permit units-added field, and both joins can be wrong where a suite was added later or a title was split after the roll date. The $350,000 to $1,000,000 example is unverifiable and receives no verdict.

Adopting Claude's matched-lot analysis of the City's assessment rolls. While 62.0 percent of classified replacement units have a higher assessed value, the large block of unverified 2024-2025 completions drops the lower bound to 42.6 percent. Therefore, the proposition is Not established.

I retain Not established. The new cross-review analysis is useful directional evidence, but it does not analyze the frozen population. It replaces the permit frame and permit year with assessment-detected candidates and last-standing-roll year, infers dwelling and title structure, uses an outcome-dependent completion heuristic and produces fractional dwelling counts. Its reported 62.0-percent classified share cannot carry the verdict because its own reported bounds span 50 percent, and those bounds omit an unknown number of lots missed by the replacement frame. The reported five-year classified share of 48.3 percent also shows that the answer is sensitive to cohort. Undivided title and lot results remain supplementary and do not rescue the unit-level proposition. The specific CAD 350,000-to-CAD 1,000,000 example remains unverified.

claims.rationale: Majority found the record silent; the lone Supported does not carry it.

reviewers.interpretation_notes: Test as run. Denominator: separately titled replacement dwellings (case 1 above) with a verified first full roll, 3,359 city-wide; a further 225 separately titled dwellings are unclassified (no verified full roll), giving bounds. Price basis: no first arm's-length sale price exists in the public record for any dwelling (Alberta sale prices are not open data), so every dwelling was priced at its total assessed value on its first verified full roll after completion, with the roll year stated per dwelling in the working file; price-year distribution 2017-2026. Household: the Statistics Canada 2021 Census median total income of households for Edmonton City (census subdivision) in 2020, $90,000, so $7,500 per month and a 30-percent threshold of $2,250 per month. Statistics Canada's classification, quoted: 'Spending less than 30% of income on shelter costs' versus 'Spending 30% or more of income on shelter costs'. Financing: 20 percent down; mortgage principal and interest on 80 percent of price at the Bank of Canada 5-year conventional mortgage rate (series V80691335, last weekly observation of July of the valuation year: 2016 4.74, 2017 4.84, 2018 5.34, 2019 5.19, 2020 4.94, 2021 4.79, 2022 6.14, 2023 6.49, 2024 6.79, 2025 6.09 percent), semi-annual compounding, 25-year amortization; property tax at the City's published residential rate for the roll year (municipal plus education plus education requisition allowance per dollar of assessed value: 2017 0.0085087, 2018 0.0088869, 2019 0.0090806, 2020 0.0093257, 2021 0.0095892, 2022 0.0093867, 2023 0.0094475, 2024 0.0101738, 2025 0.0101391, 2026 0.0103637); utilities as a fixed modelled allowance of $377.67 per month, being Statistics Canada Table 11-10-0222-01, Alberta, 'Water, fuel and electricity for principal accommodation', average $4,532 per household in 2023 (the most recent Survey of Household Spending year released, on 2025-05-21), divided by twelve; it is not any dwelling's bill. Condominium fees: no fee is published in the assessment record, so no fee is included for any of the 189 dwellings on the cohort lots whose permits are condominium row-house or semi-detached types; count stated as not included. RESULT: 2,968 of 3,359 = 88.4 percent of separately titled replacement dwellings require 30 percent or more of the modelled household's income; lower bound (225 unclassified treated as meeting the threshold) 2,968/3,584 = 82.8 percent; upper bound 89.1 percent. Median price $638,000 (Q1 $463,000, Q3 $855,250); median monthly shelter cost $3,948 (median components: principal and interest $3,070, property tax $494, utilities $377.67); median cost-to-income ratio 0.526 (Q1 0.392, Q3 0.690, range 0.06-4.40). Mature subset: 2,891/3,279 = 88.2 percent. Lot-level rules among separately titled dwellings: every-dwelling 1,882/2,002 lots = 94.0 percent; at-least-one 94.8 percent. Excluded single-title multi-unit dwelling units: 3,244, which is 49.1 percent of the 6,603 classified replacement dwelling units, building-average value per unit median $265,250 (Q1 $216,365, Q3 $312,063); their rental affordability is not tested because CMHC average-rent cells make no adjustment for utilities and no contract rents are published. SENSITIVITIES (each labelled, none carries the verdict): without the utility allowance 2,718/3,359 = 80.9 percent, verdict unchanged; 30-year amortization 85.7 percent (available for insured mortgages to first-time buyers and to all buyers of newly constructed homes from 2024-12-15 under SOR/2025-55; a 20-percent-down conventional mortgage is not insured, so the 30-year case is a modelling sensitivity only); regulatory minimum down payment (5 percent to $500,000, 10 percent on the portion to $1.5 million, 20 percent at or above $1.5 million) with CMHC premium added to the loan (4.00 percent at LTV over 90, 3.10 percent over 85, 2.80 percent over 80; insurance is available only under $1.5 million) 94.4 percent; Canadian Income Survey 2024 median total income for Edmonton CMA economic families and persons not in economic families, $91,100 (a family-unit figure, not a household figure) 87.6 percent; census 2021 two-or-more-person households $112,000: 77.8 percent; one-person households $47,600: 98.6 percent. By price roll year: 2017 97.9 percent, 2018 87.4, 2019 93.4, 2020 74.1, 2021 81.8, 2022 88.7, 2023 95.6, 2024 95.4, 2025 99.4, 2026 100 (50 of 50). Bedroom-count breakdown cannot be produced: the assessment record and permits do not give bedrooms. Note on the brief's income rule: the fixed 2020 income is set against prices dated 2016-2025 without indexing; that overstates failure for later years and understates it for earlier ones. It does not change the verdict here (even the 2020-dated cohort fails at 74 percent), but the editor may want the income indexed in a future revision. Comparators, each separate: same-neighbourhood median price in the same year could not be built from public data (assessment data has no sale prices; RAE does not publish neighbourhood medians openly) and is missing; regional new-construction comparator is missing (CMHC absorbed-price series was not retrieved); city-wide resale context only: RAE July 2026 average prices detached $585,726, semi-detached $425,329, row/townhouse $292,756, apartment condominium $214,521. Rent context only: CMHC October 2025 Edmonton average two-bedroom rent $1,603, vacancy 3.8 percent; no property-level rent is published for any replacement, so the rent comparator carries nothing here.

The required denominator (separately titled replacement dwellings in the matched set) cannot be identified without the missing joined dataset from Claim 1. Furthermore, first arm's-length sale prices or first full assessment values for this specific matched set are unavailable in aggregate public reports.

This is a hypothetical purchase model, not evidence about actual occupants, purchaser incomes or rent affordability. Aggregate new-home and benchmark-price evidence is directionally informative but cannot replace the matched separately titled dwelling denominator. Single-title multi-unit dwellings were treated as excluded, not as affordable or unaffordable.

round2_positions.interpretation_notes: My position is unchanged. On 3,359 separately titled replacement dwellings, 2,968 (88.4 percent) exceed the threshold; median price $638,000, median monthly cost $3,948 against a $2,250 limit. Bounds over the full denominator are 82.8 to 89.1 percent, so the lower bound clears 50 percent by a wide margin and the verdict is Supported. Every price is an assessed value; no first arm's-length sale price exists in the open record for any dwelling, and the report must say the sale series covered zero cases. gpt's mortgage-rate point is fair and I answer it: the Bank's 2019 notice says the discontinued monthly rate was the last weekly Wednesday rate of the month, and my rule takes the last weekly observation of the price month from V80691335, which reproduces that definition. The result is robust to the sensitivities I ran: $112,000 two-or-more-person household income gives 77.8 percent, the 2020-dated price cohort gives 74.1 percent. Removing the $377.67 allowance from the median cost leaves about $3,570, still far above $2,250, so the no-utility sensitivity cannot flip the verdict, though its exact share must be stated in the report. The 3,244 single-title units (49 percent of all replacement units) are excluded and their rental affordability is untested, not failed. Two cautions on my own run. Posted rates overstate contract rates, and applying a 2020 income to 2025 prices pushes cost ratios up; both bias toward failing, and neither could plausibly move an 88 percent share below half. And the separately-titled test is the account-count proxy from Claim 1, so a row house wrongly counted as single-title is missing from this denominator rather than wrongly in it. The City's own 2024 report reaches a compatible conclusion on a resale benchmark under easier financing, which is context and not verification. Nothing here tests renting, tenure, the causal effect of infill, or the City's affordable-housing definition.

round2_positions.changed_why: Claude's successful operationalization of the assessment data provided the price basis for separately titled replacements, yielding a lower bound of 82.8 percent that clearly clears the 50 percent threshold.
round2_positions.interpretation_notes: Claude's purchase model calculation establishes a lower bound of 82.8 percent failing the threshold. I agree with Claude that the lack of public sale prices means we use the assessed value as directed by the brief. The result overwhelmingly supports the claim.

I retain Not established. Claude's proxy model is strong directional evidence: it reports 2,968 of 3,359 classified separately titled candidates, 88.4 percent, above the threshold, with a reported lower bound of 82.8 percent among 3,584 candidate dwellings. That calculation still inherits Claim 1's nonconforming assessment-detected frame and inferred title classification. It also uses assessed value for every dwelling without establishing whether a first arm's-length sale existed. The reported bound therefore covers only its inferred candidate set, not the complete denominator fixed by the brief. The calculation supports concern about purchase affordability but does not prove the required majority. It does not test rent affordability or actual occupant costs.
